data.body:
DECISION + EVIDENCE for the criterion "decide and record whether an exhausted push race should be red or a PUSH_PENDING-style non-red notice, resolving it against docs/concurrency.md:297-300".

## Evidence 1 — the events WERE re-derived

Every one of the four failed runs was followed by a SUCCESSFUL reconciler push within
~20 minutes (`git log origin/tickets`, commits `chore: sync events from rebar reconciler
[run <id>]`):

    failed 30503669644 @ 2026-07-30T00:45:55Z -> next push 01:04:06Z (+18 min, run 30504126058)
    failed 30510284129 @ 2026-07-30T03:06:34Z -> next push 03:25:44Z (+19 min, run 30510768428)
    failed 30515516036 @ 2026-07-30T05:02:44Z -> next push 05:18:52Z (+16 min, run 30515857104)
    failed 30585738860 @ 2026-07-30T22:03:07Z -> next push 22:24:05Z (+21 min, run 30586410591)

## Evidence 2 — no duplicates, no orphans

`rebar bridge-fsck` reports **"No issues found."** No duplicate binding for any
`local_id`, no orphaned mappings, no stale SYNCs. (The `absent_in_window_unprobed`
lines are windowing artifacts explicitly documented as NOT deletion signals, ADR 0028
§1.) So a lost push did not cause a duplicate Jira issue, which was the specific risk
the criterion named.

Conclusion on the facts: an exhausted push race is BENIGN. Nothing was permanently
lost; the reconciler re-derived the state on its next pass, which is exactly what a
drift-healing reconciler is for.

## Decision: KEEP IT RED. Rationale, resolved against the doc rather than by preference.

`docs/concurrency.md:297-300` says a failed push "never fails the caller — it warns,
leaves local commits intact, and the branch stays diverged. `rebar fsck` surfaces that
divergence as a `PUSH_PENDING` notice ... so it is not silent."

Read closely, that posture is CONDITIONAL on a surface: it is safe to not fail the
caller **because** the local commits survive and `fsck` reports the divergence later.
Both halves of that condition hold for the library client on a developer's disk. On a
GitHub Actions runner NEITHER holds — the container is destroyed at job end, so there
are no surviving local commits to stay diverged and no subsequent `fsck` to surface a
`PUSH_PENDING`. The doc's guarantee that the failure "is not silent" has no mechanism
in this context.

So exiting non-red here would not reproduce the library's behaviour; it would produce
the one thing the doc is careful to avoid — a silent loss. With no notice channel, the
job's exit status is the only signal that exists.

The second reason is that the fix changes what a red MEANS. Before, exhaustion was the
expected outcome of ordinary contention (~12% of runs by the measured model). After
re-pushing immediately and spending the final merge, exhausting six attempts is no
longer something normal contention produces — so a red now indicates something genuinely
unusual (credentials revoked, branch protection changed, a pathological burst) rather
than routine traffic. Silencing it would trade a rare true positive for permanent
blindness to a class of real failure.

## What would justify revisiting

Flip to non-red IF a `PUSH_PENDING` equivalent is added for the ephemeral context — e.g.
the step emits a `::warning::` plus a durable marker (a bridge alert or a ticket) that a
later pass or the heartbeat canary can surface. At that point the doc's condition is
satisfied in CI and its posture should be followed. Without that surface, red is the
faithful reading of the contract, not a deviation from it.
